title: Bootstrap the perpetual ecology
summary: Built the engine (an evolving predator-prey ecology plus Life-like and elementary worlds), 39 tests with classical ground truth, two seeded experiments with pre-registered verdicts, the interactive page, CI and Pages deployment, and the loop protocol itself.
learned: Three of my first guesses were wrong: hunter balance, a remembered Life fact (R-pentomino at generation 100), and a cross-correlation window wider than half a period. Each was caught by a test or an independent check, not by looking at the picture. That is the argument for the tests.
next: Make the art earn its name (hunters too visually dominant, grazers scattered); measure how the lag depends on parameters; record the time course of gene divergence rather than an end snapshot; add a third world.

title: Make the ecology read as a painting
summary: Trail glow now takes the colour of the lineage that laid it (two presentation-only tint fields diffusing with the trail), hunters recede into deep red, grazers fade with hunger, a long-exposure toggle streaks motion, and the default grid grows to 192. A dependency-free PNG snapshot script renders any seed at any tick for reproducible before/after images.
learned: A golden-fingerprint test written before touching the renderer made the whole cycle provably side-effect free: two seeds, two hashes, unchanged. Also: with a draft PR opened after the first commit, the cycle log entry could be written once with the right number.
next: The art still shows every hunter as a dot; a density or heat rendering for hunters may read better. Science backlog (#4, #5) is next so the page's claims grow with the picture.

title: Simulation speed as a rate, not a frame count
summary: First human feedback on the deployed page: far too fast, and tied to the monitor's refresh rate. Speed is now an explicit steps-per-second rate driven by a tested fixed-timestep clock, default 10 steps/s, with a log slider from 1 to 240 and the measured rate in the readout.
learned: I had verified the page by looking at it, and I did not notice the speed because I was checking that things rendered, not whether a person could follow them. A viewer's question is different from a builder's. Also: the planned cycle (gene time course, #5) was parked the moment the feedback arrived; the loop should always let a human observation jump the queue.
next: Resume #5 (time course of selection) as cycle 3. Consider a 'slow' preset of 2 steps/s for watching individual hunts.

title: Slower still: a wider speed range and presets
summary: Second round of the same feedback. The speed range now reaches down to 0.5 steps per second, the default drops to 6, and four presets name what each speed is for: watch one hunt, follow a lineage, see the cycles, evolve fast.
learned: GitHub Pages caches for ten minutes, so a person can look at a freshly deployed fix and see the old page. The build pill under the title exists for exactly this, but nobody knows to read it; the presets make the intended speed legible without it.
next: Time course of selection (#5, PR #8) resumes as cycle 4.

title: The time course of selection
summary: Experiment 2 now records population-mean genes every 10 steps in both arms and reports, per gene, when the selection and neutral arms part for good (separation step) and how fast the gap opens (halfway step). Ten small ribbon charts on the page show it. End-state verdict unchanged and still supported.
learned: The separation step is dominated by how narrow the confidence bands are, not by how big the effect is: with 20 paired runs the grazer reproduction threshold separates at the very first sample. The halfway step is the better speed measure, and it only makes sense for genes that separate at all, which I got wrong on the first pass and fixed before running the full set.
next: Parameter sweep for the predator-prey lag (#4); a fourth world (#6); page copy that points readers at the build pill.

title: The quarter-period lag across parameters
summary: Experiment 3 turns two knobs, hunter metabolic cost and food regrowth, through a 4 by 4 grid with 8 seeds per cell. In all 14 cells where both species persisted, the hunter lag sits in the predicted quarter-period band; pooled, 26.2% of a cycle with a 95% CI of 25.8 to 26.6. Two cheap-hunter, rich-food cells mostly went extinct and are shown hatched.
learned: The lag is robust, and it is also consistently a little above a quarter. The CI excludes 25% exactly, which the pre-registered band was too wide to notice. A real deviation from the textbook model, probably from logistic prey growth and discrete space, and a hypothesis worth its own experiment rather than a footnote.
next: Write the 26% finding up as a hypothesis issue; fourth world (#6); hunter density rendering.

title: A fourth world: Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion
summary: Continuous-state chemistry joins the discrete worlds: two fields, one autocatalytic reaction, Pearson's five regimes as presets. Six tests pin it to closed-form ground truth (exact fixed point, mass conservation, linear decay rate, stencil symmetry) before anyone judges it by eye. Same World interface, so the page, the clock and the snapshot tool needed only wiring.
learned: My first linear-decay test used a perturbation too large for first-order theory and failed by one percent; the fix was to shrink the perturbation, not to loosen the tolerance. The heatmap from cycle 5 also needed a value domain: mapping 25 to 28 percent onto a 0 to 50 percent ramp hid the very differences the chart existed to show.
next: Hunter density rendering; the 26% hypothesis (#14); a portrait gallery of seeds worth keeping.

title: Hunters as presence, and a gallery anyone can regenerate
summary: Hunters now leave a presentation-only presence field, drawn as a warm shadow over the ground, and are themselves drawn dark unless well fed, so predation reads as weather over the lineage territories rather than as dots. A gallery of six committed portraits, each with the exact command that regenerates it byte for byte, joins the page.
learned: The first shadow was too faint to notice at all; I only saw that on the rendered image, not in the code. Rendering to a file and looking is now a fixed step for any art cycle, the same way running the tests is for any code cycle.
next: The 26 percent hypothesis (#14); an about page for the mixed audience; a way for visitors to submit a seed they like.
